plannerAnswers.question: What did you like most about this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: It gives real design authority and then makes that authority checkable. Genre and perspective are mine to pick, but the engine kit and the hub protocol are real, linked and runnable, and the 'This computer' section says exactly what exists and what the stand-ins are. That let me prove the risky parts before writing them down: the single file from file://, a shoulder camera, custom characters on the hero rig, and shared-world co-op through the harness. The plan could then mark facts as verified instead of hoping.

plannerAnswers.question: What was confusing?
plannerAnswers.answer: Three things. First, 'Follow the hub for multiplayer integration into ai-hub as well as for the game on its own': this can mean the game must simply still run outside a session, or that it needs its own multiplayer outside the hub. The hub README only supports the first, so I planned for both, with a same-computer party and WebRTC invite codes. Second, 'Capture what makes the source distinctive (its world, characters...)' sits next to 'Build an original game': it isn't stated how close an analogue may get, and my first villain came out too close to a specific character, so I redesigned him. Third, I don't know which models or effort levels will build from the plan, which makes it hard to size the scope. The engine guide's 'ES modules don't load from file://' also reads as conflicting with 'Prefer file://' until you find that an inlined module bundle works.

plannerAnswers.question: What was the hardest thing to do?
plannerAnswers.answer: Making a plan big enough to be a feature-complete demo of a very varied source, yet still buildable by an agent who can't ask me anything. That meant inventing an original counterpart for each signature idea rather than renaming it, then writing it down concretely enough to need no follow-up: maps that I checked for reachability, numbers, a network protocol, actual script lines. Then I had to decide what can be cut cleanly when 'no stubs' and 'show all features' pull against a real risk of running out of road. The engine also has no shoulder camera, no character art path except its hero, and a font without some punctuation, so each of those needed a tested workaround before the plan could depend on it.

plannerAnswers.question: What would you change in this prompt?
plannerAnswers.answer: State plainly whether the game needs multiplayer outside AI Hub and, if so, how players are expected to connect. Add a target length or size for the demo, such as 30 to 45 minutes, since 'long enough to show all features' can mean ten minutes or two hours. Say which models and effort levels will build from the plan, so the director can size it. Add one line on how close to the source's characters and levels an original game may get. I would also tell planners that they may run proofs of concept in their folder, and clean them up, because that was the most valuable hour of this stage.
